Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. Alternatively, in automated health care, control should be passed on to human doctors when the conﬁdence of a dis- ease diagnosis network is low (Jiang et al., 2012). Specif- ically, a network should provide a calibrated conﬁdence measure in addition to its prediction. In other words, the probability associated with the predicted class label should reﬂect its ground truth correctness likelihood. Calibrated conﬁdence estimates are also important for model interpretability. Humans have a natural cognitive in- tuition for probabilities (Cosmides & Tooby, 1996). Good conﬁdence estimates provide a valuable extra bit of infor- mation to establish trustworthiness with the user – espe- cially for neural networks, whose classiﬁcation decisions are often difﬁcult to interpret. Further, good probability estimates can be used to incorporate neural networks into other probabilistic models. reviews on the PHQ-9 published to date, approxi mately 800 articles evaluated the psychometric properties of the PHQ -9 using the CTT model (4,5,8,21-29). CTT -based techniques could provide inaccurate diagnoses and do not consider the heterogeneity in each specific item (30, 31). Currently, these CCT-based methods are being complemented and, in some cases, replaced by item response theory (IRT) approaches, considered by many researchers to be the "measurement paradigm of the 21st century" (19, 32 -35). IRT -based models offer several advantages over CTT and are considered the most appropriate and robust methods for assessing the psychometric properties of screening scales such as the PHQ-9 (36,37). The idea of IRT is that test -response behavior (i.e., solving an item or choosing a specific category) can be explained by underlying person parameters (latent ability or trait) and item parameters (difficulty) (34). The relationship between the latent trait and probability of response to a given item can be expressed by different estimation models for both dichotomous and polytomous items (32,38). This approach estimates item and person parameters from the obtained data and is considered independent of the sample and test (39). In addition, IRT-based models provide a richer description of the performance of each item, greater detail on the accuracy of a measure, and when assumptions are met, scores are item - independent and invariant across different samples (33,34,40,41). Consequently, the use of IRT models may increase the validity and utility of depression screening when the PHQ-9 is used in culturally diverse settings (42,43). Available Knowledge/Review of the Literature According to the U.S. Preventative Services Task Force (USPSTF), depression is among the leading causes of disability in individuals 15 years of age and older (Siu & U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), 2016). By 2020, depressive disorders are predicted to be the second leading cause of disability and death (Soltani, Smith, Beck, & Johnson, 2014). Prevalence of depression among college students accounts for approximately 16.7% and is more than twice as common among college students compared to the general population (Liu et al., 2019; English & Campbell, 2019). Thus, depression is highly prevalent and appears to be increasing. Depression is one of the leading health concerns in college population, yet roughly half of college students with depression receive treatment (English & Campbell, 2019). Mental health among college students affects important outcomes such as social connectedness, academic performance, academic retention, and future economic productivity, which should be a significant concern for certain stakeholders such as campus administrators, college professors, and parents (Lipson, Gaddis, Heinze, & Eisenberg, 2015; Ebert et al., 2018). In addition, depression has been associated with increased health care costs such as emergency department visits and inpatient hospitalizations (Wright et al., 2015).
